lesson_title: The Planet Runs on Three Escalators
hook_text: Why do all the world's worst deserts sit in one neat ring at 30 degrees? The sky has escalators.
clip_script: Picture the atmosphere between the equator and the South Pole as three escalator loops in a giant shopping mall, each one endlessly cycling air up, across, down and back. Loop one serves the tropics: over the equator the ground bakes all year, air rides up, wrings out its rain and drifts poleward near the ceiling. By about 30 degrees south it has chilled, grown heavy and steps off downward — and coming-down air is drying air. That is exactly why a ring of the world's harshest deserts circles the globe at 30 degrees: the Sahara, the Namib, the Kalahari, the Australian interior, all standing under the down escalator. Loop two freeloads through the middle latitudes, dragged around by its neighbours, and its floor-level wind is the westerlies — the belt that flings winter cold fronts at the southern Cape. Loop three slides icy air off the pole until it collides with the westerlies and both are forced upward. Now the sentence that unlocks our country: the whole escalator hall is on rollers. It trundles about five degrees north in our winter, so the cold fronts reach the south-western Cape and soak it in June. It rolls south in summer, the fronts miss us, and moist tropical air floods the plateau instead. One moving machine — and one country ends up with two completely different rainy seasons.
visual_style: Three glowing escalator loops in cross-section between equator and pole, a desert ring lighting up under the descending limb at 30 degrees, then the whole hall sliding north and south over a South African map while month labels roll past.
mood: Big-machine wonder with a satisfying local payoff.
pacing: Steady climb through the three loops, sharp beat on the desert ring, brisk seasonal slide to close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and predict any latitude's winds and rain straight off the model.
